strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated alternative to reconstruction-based diffusion anomaly detection: invert a test sample through a DDIM/PF-ODE trajectory and score the resulting latent, reducing inference to 2-5 network evaluations.

The method is simple and computationally attractive. Reported latency is much lower than most compared diffusion-based baselines, and the inversion-vs-reconstruction ablation in Table 4 supports the claim that reconstruction methods are sensitive to denoising start point while inversion can work with very few steps.

Using pretrained backbone feature space for diffusion is sensible for industrial anomaly detection, and the paper evaluates on two standard benchmarks, MVTecAD and VisA, with both image-level and pixel-level AUC reported.

The manuscript identifies an important phenomenon for likelihood-based generative anomaly detection: negative log-likelihood can reverse-score normal and anomalous samples in high-dimensional settings, and the paper provides empirical evidence of this issue.
weaknesses: The central framing as direct latent likelihood evaluation is not fully supported by the final method. Table 4 shows NLL performance collapses as the number of inversion steps increases, and the final scoring function adds a spatial norm-difference heuristic rather than relying on Gaussian prior likelihood alone. This weakens the main technical claim that prior density itself is an effective anomaly score.

There are potentially serious evaluation protocol issues. The paper states that results are reported from the best-performing checkpoints and Ours* tunes S over {2,3,4,5}, but it does not describe a validation set or unsupervised model-selection rule. On benchmarks such as MVTecAD, choosing checkpoints or S based on test anomaly labels would substantially inflate performance.

The abstract claim of 0.991 AUC at 15 FPS appears inconsistent with Table 2: 99.1 image-level AUC corresponds to Ours* with 85 ms latency, while 64 ms latency corresponds to Ours with 97.3 image-level AUC. This matters because the main claimed contribution is the speed-AUC trade-off.

The comparison scope is narrow and somewhat favorable. The paper mostly compares against diffusion-based methods, while industrial anomaly detection has strong non-diffusion baselines such as EfficientAD, PatchCore, PaDiM/FastFlow-style methods, etc. This limits support for the broader state-of-the-art speed-AUC claim.

Performance is mixed outside the best MVTec image-level setting. On VisA, the untuned method has low average image-level AUC (79.1), and even Ours* remains below several baselines in image-level AUC. On MVTecAD, pixel-level AUC is substantially worse than most diffusion baselines despite good image-level AUC.

The technical justification for dropping the Jacobian term is weak. Equation 16 explicitly requires a change-of-variables correction, and the manuscript says it is omitted under an Euler-approximated ODE setting, but does not provide a convincing derivation or conditions under which the resulting score should preserve anomaly ranking.

Important reproducibility details are missing: exact feature layer(s) from EfficientNet-B4, input resolution, UNet architecture, batch size, learning rate, weight decay, hardware, training time, seed variation, anomaly-score normalization procedure, and whether normalization uses training-only statistics. These details are necessary to reproduce both accuracy and latency.

The writing has repeated paragraphs and some imprecise notation, especially around the feature-space diffusion description and Algorithm 1. The algorithm also appears inconsistent with the earlier norm definition and does not clearly define how the final normalized score is computed.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful limitation of diffusion-based anomaly detection: reconstruction-based inference can be slow and sensitive to the denoising start/noise level. The proposed inversion-style inference is simple and potentially useful if validated more rigorously.

The method achieves low reported latency among the compared diffusion-based methods: 64-96 ms versus hundreds or thousands of milliseconds for several diffusion baselines, while retaining reasonable image-level AUC on MVTecAD when S is tuned.

The manuscript includes comparisons on two standard industrial anomaly benchmarks, MVTecAD and VisA, and provides a focused ablation contrasting reconstruction-based inference with inversion-based scoring over different step counts.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is not well supported. The paper motivates direct latent likelihood under a Gaussian prior, but Table 4 shows NLL performance collapses as the number of steps increases, e.g. MVTecAD image AUC drops from 96.9 at S=3 to 59.5 at S=1000. The final method therefore relies substantially on a spatial norm/range heuristic, not the claimed direct latent likelihood evaluation.

The likelihood formulation is incomplete and potentially misleading. The method omits the Jacobian term in the PF-ODE change of variables, yet still interprets prior density as an anomaly score. The argument that this is acceptable is empirical and weak, especially because the paper itself observes a reverse-scoring problem where normal samples receive lower likelihood than anomalous samples.

The evaluation is not convincing enough for the stated claims. On MVTecAD, the fixed S=2 result is only 97.3 image AUC / 93.7 pixel AUC, below several diffusion baselines; the tuned Ours* improves image AUC to 99.1 but pixel AUC remains 94.8, well below many baselines around 98. On VisA, fixed S=2 is poor at 79.1 image AUC / 87.4 pixel AUC, and even Ours* remains below GLAD/DDAD/DAD in image-level AUC.

The paper claims a new state-of-the-art speed-AUC tradeoff, but compares mainly against diffusion-based methods and does not seriously compare with strong non-diffusion industrial anomaly detectors such as PatchCore-style memory methods or EfficientAD-like real-time methods. This weakens the usefulness and positioning of the contribution for CVPR.

Several fairness issues are unclear. The paper reports best-performing checkpoints and Ours* tunes S in {2,3,4,5}; it is not specified what validation protocol is used or whether anomaly labels/test information influence checkpoint or S selection. This is especially concerning because the paper criticizes prior work for tuning perturbation steps.

The scoring procedure is under-specified and may leak distributional information. Algorithm 1 uses Normalize(||x||2) and Normalize(range of spatial norms), but the normalization statistics are not defined. It is unclear whether normalization is per image, per class, training-set based, or test-set based.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a method whose performance depends on implementation choices. The manuscript does not adequately specify the EfficientNet feature layer(s), input resolution, UNet architecture, optimizer hyperparameters such as learning rate/batch size/weight decay, hardware for latency, or random-seed variability.

The writing and presentation have notable issues: duplicated paragraphs in Section 4.3, inconsistent notation in Algorithm 1 versus Eq. 17, awkward or incorrect claims such as p_theta(x_T) for a fixed Gaussian prior, and limited qualitative evidence for localization despite reporting pixel-level AUC.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful departure from reconstruction-based diffusion anomaly detection: invert inputs to a diffusion latent via a short DDIM/PF-ODE trajectory and score the resulting latent, avoiding iterative denoising and timestep selection.

The central practical claim is well motivated and supported by experiments: with only 2-5 function evaluations, the method achieves strong image-level AUC on MVTecAD and much lower latency than most diffusion-based baselines (64-96 ms versus hundreds or thousands of ms).

The paper includes meaningful ablations comparing inversion to reconstruction under different step counts and denoising starting points. These results help substantiate the claim that inversion is less sensitive to perturbation-step tuning.
The feature-space diffusion formulation is sensible for industrial anomaly detection and connects well to common practice in the area, where ImageNet-pretrained features are often crucial.
The authors are reasonably transparent about an important failure mode: direct Gaussian NLL can suffer from reverse scoring, and the spatial norm score is empirically shown to mitigate this issue.
weaknesses: The accuracy evidence is mixed. On MVTecAD, image-level AUC is competitive but not best among diffusion methods, while pixel-level AUC is substantially below several baselines on average. On VisA, the fixed-step version is weak for image-level detection, and even the tuned version remains below GLAD/DAD/DDAD in image-level AUC.

The claimed state-of-the-art speed-AUC trade-off is not fully established because comparisons are mostly restricted to diffusion-based methods. Since the method uses pretrained backbone features, stronger non-diffusion industrial anomaly detection baselines such as PatchCore, EfficientAD, CFLOW/MSFlow-style methods, and recent memory/feature methods are important for judging practical usefulness.

The theoretical justification is incomplete. The method deliberately drops the Jacobian term from the likelihood, then ultimately relies on a heuristic spatial norm-difference score. This may work empirically, but the paper does not provide a rigorous explanation of when the latent score should be valid or why the min-max spatial norm statistic is the right correction.

Some evaluation choices may inflate results or reduce clarity. The paper reports best-performing checkpoints for fairness with some prior work, and Ours* tunes S in {2,3,4,5}; it is not clear whether this tuning uses validation data independent of the test anomalies. This matters because unsupervised anomaly detection is sensitive to model selection protocols.

Reproducibility details are under-specified: the exact EfficientNet feature layer(s), feature dimensionality, input resolution, learning rate, batch size, hardware used for latency, and normalization used in the final score are not sufficiently clear. Algorithm 1 also contains notation inconsistencies between norm maps, summed norms, and the final image-level score.

The presentation has several rough spots, including duplicated text in Section 4.3, table/algorithm notation issues, and some overstatements about eliminating tuning despite the existence of the tuned Ours* setting. These are fixable but currently make parts of the method harder to reproduce and assess.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful shift for diffusion-based anomaly detection: scoring the inverted latent/noise state rather than performing expensive reconstruction. This directly targets a real limitation of prior diffusion AD methods, namely the sensitivity and cost of denoising-based reconstruction.

The empirical results are fairly broad for the target problem. The method is evaluated on MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD, and additionally BMAD in the supplement, with both image-level and pixel-level metrics plus throughput measurements.

The main efficiency claim is well supported: the reported FPS is substantially higher than prior diffusion-based methods across the industrial benchmarks, while maintaining competitive or better image-level AUROC, especially on VisA and MPDD.

The ablations are informative. The paper studies inversion versus reconstruction under different step counts, feature-space encoders, diffusion backbones, plug-in use with other diffusion AD methods, and scoring variants. These analyses help isolate why the method works and where performance comes from.

The method is conceptually simple and potentially useful in practice: it requires only a few inversion steps, avoids timestep perturbation tuning, and can be combined with existing diffusion AD models at inference time.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is somewhat overstated. The method still relies heavily on pretrained discriminative feature encoders such as EfficientNet; Table 6 shows large performance drops with VAE or ResNet features. Thus the gain is not solely due to the diffusion/inversion paradigm, and the diffusion component’s unique contribution over direct feature-norm or density baselines is not fully isolated.

The comparison to prior work is not always convincing. Several baselines appear to be taken from prior reports rather than re-run under a uniform implementation and hardware setup, while FPS is measured for the proposed method on an RTX 4090 with batch size 64. This makes the magnitude of the efficiency advantage difficult to interpret precisely.

The paper’s claims of state-of-the-art detection performance are too broad. On MVTecAD multi-class, InvAD is faster but has lower mAD than OmiAD and weaker pixel AP/F1; on MVTecAD single-class its average pixel AUROC is below several diffusion baselines. The contribution is stronger as an efficiency/accuracy tradeoff than as a uniformly best detector.

The anomaly scoring formulation is not presented as cleanly as it should be. The abstract/table describe log p(x_T), the method section emphasizes norm differences, Algorithm 1 uses an abs(max-min)+sum score, and the supplement discusses NLL+Abs. This inconsistency makes it harder to assess the exact scoring rule and reproduce the reported numbers.

The theoretical justification is plausible but incomplete. The argument that normal samples map to high-density prior regions and anomalies to low-density regions under approximate DDIM inversion is intuitive, but there is little analysis of when this holds, especially under very coarse Euler inversion with only three steps and in pretrained feature space.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released code in the manuscript, very large model/training requirements for the main DiT-gigant setting, and incomplete details about baseline evaluation protocols. The supplement gives useful hyperparameters, but not enough to ensure faithful reproduction of all comparisons.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful limitation of diffusion-based anomaly detection: reconstruction-based methods can be slow and sensitive to perturbation/noise timestep choices. The proposed inversion-based framing is a clear and potentially useful alternative direction.

The method is simple at inference time: extract pretrained features, run a small number of DDIM inversion steps, and score the inferred latent map. This simplicity is attractive compared with more elaborate reconstruction or distillation pipelines.

The empirical section covers several standard industrial anomaly detection datasets, reports both image-level and pixel-level metrics, and includes useful ablations over inversion steps, feature encoders, diffusion architectures, and scoring variants.

The reported throughput is strong among the compared diffusion-based methods, e.g. 88.1 FPS on MVTecAD and 74.1 FPS on VisA in the multi-class setting, while maintaining competitive image-level AUROC.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is not sufficiently justified. The paper argues that normal samples map to high-density regions and anomalous samples to low-density regions under deterministic PF-ODE/DDIM inversion, but this is not established theoretically and is exactly where likelihood/typicality failures for generative models are known to occur. The final scoring rule is a heuristic patch rather than a convincing resolution of this issue.

The novelty appears incremental. The method combines DDIM inversion, pretrained feature-space modeling, and norm/likelihood-style anomaly scoring, all of which are closely related to prior diffusion OOD/anomaly detection ideas. The paper overstates the paradigm shift without clearly isolating what is technically new beyond using a few inversion steps and a particular score aggregation.

The scoring formulation is internally inconsistent. The abstract/table describe scoring by log p_theta(x_T), the methodology first discusses log-likelihood, then uses channelwise Euclidean norm, Algorithm 1 uses abs(max(A)-min(A)) plus a sum over A, and the supplement reports NLL+Abs as the proposed scoring scheme. This makes the actual method harder to verify and weakens reproducibility.

The empirical evidence does not fully support the strongest claims. On MVTecAD multi-class, InvAD has lower mAD than OmiAD and weaker pixel-level AP/F1 than several baselines, despite claims of state-of-the-art detection performance. In single-class MVTecAD, InvAD is not best on average for either image- or pixel-level AUROC. The contribution is mainly speed among diffusion baselines, not uniformly superior accuracy.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete and potentially misleading. The paper mentions non-diffusion EfficientAD exceeding 200 FPS but does not include it in the main quantitative tables. InvAD also uses a very large diffusion model in some settings, with training on 8 H200 GPUs for 300 epochs; inference FPS alone does not characterize the practical cost of the approach.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is unclear. Many baseline numbers appear drawn from prior papers, while FPS is measured under the authors' setup for some methods but unavailable or heterogeneous for others. Batch-size effects are acknowledged, yet not normalized carefully enough for a robust efficiency claim.

The plug-and-play/generalizability claim is weakly supported. Only two methods are tested, and adding InvAD to DeCoDiff reduces AUROC substantially on both MVTecAD and VisA. This does not convincingly demonstrate model-agnostic applicability.

The method relies heavily on pretrained feature extractors; the ablation shows large drops with weaker encoders. This complicates attribution of gains to the diffusion inversion mechanism rather than to the backbone representation and raises questions about whether a non-diffusion detector on the same features would be similarly effective or faster.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript includes some hyperparameters, but the project/code fields are blank, implementation details for exact feature layers and scoring normalization are insufficient, and no variance over seeds or confidence intervals are reported.

Presentation has several issues that affect technical clarity: claims alternate between three and four benchmarks, there are typos and awkward phrasing, and some tables/algorithm descriptions do not match the surrounding text. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they make the contribution harder to assess.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful shift for diffusion-based anomaly detection: replacing reconstruction/denoising with DDIM inversion and scoring the inferred latent under the diffusion prior. This directly targets two real pain points in prior diffusion AD methods: timestep/noise-strength tuning and expensive multi-step reconstruction.

The empirical case is strong overall. On multi-class MVTecAD, VisA, and MPDD, the method achieves very competitive or best image-level AU-ROC/AP/F1 while substantially improving throughput, e.g. 88.1 FPS on MVTecAD versus 39.4 for OmiAD and much lower FPS for most diffusion baselines.

The ablations are meaningful. The comparison against reconstruction across diffusion steps and perturbation ratios supports the claim that inversion is less sensitive to timestep choices, and the backbone/architecture ablations clarify that feature quality matters more than diffusion architecture choice.

The supplementary material adds useful reproducibility details, including dataset statistics, preprocessing, model hyperparameters, training schedule, hardware, and additional results on single-class VisA and BMAD.

The method is practically appealing because it improves efficiency without requiring adversarial distillation or explicit reconstruction, and it can be incorporated into some existing diffusion-based AD pipelines.
weaknesses: The strongest claims of state-of-the-art performance need nuance. The method is excellent on image-level detection and speed, but pixel-level results are mixed: on MVTecAD, OmiAD has better pixel AP/F1/AU-PRO than InvAD, and in the single-class table InvAD has lower average pixel AU-ROC than several diffusion baselines.

The scoring formulation is not fully consistent or theoretically settled. The main text emphasizes norm-based scoring, Table 1 says the scoring scheme is log p_theta(x_T), Algorithm 1 uses abs(max-min)+sum(A), and the supplement says NLL+Abs is the final scheme. This ambiguity affects clarity and reproducibility.

The conceptual justification that normal samples map to high-density latent regions while anomalous samples map to low-density regions is plausible but not rigorously established under learned approximate score models and very coarse three-step Euler inversion. The empirical evidence helps, but the theoretical framing is stronger than what is proven.

The method depends heavily on pretrained feature encoders; EfficientNet-B4 is crucial for the best results, while VAE/ResNet features perform much worse. This makes the contribution partly a feature-space AD method plus diffusion inversion, and the paper could better separate the gains from the backbone versus the diffusion component.

The efficiency comparison is encouraging but not completely normalized. FPS is measured with batch size 64 on an RTX 4090, while many baseline numbers appear taken from prior reports or different implementations/settings. Training cost is also high, with large DiT variants and H200-scale training resources, which weakens the practical efficiency story.

The plug-and-play generalizability claim is only partially supported. Adding InvAD to DeCoDiff improves FPS but reduces AU-ROC by about 2-3 points on MVTecAD/VisA; the positive MDM result is promising but the evidence base is small.

There are some presentation issues, including typos and unclear notation in Algorithm 1, and the project/code fields are blank in the manuscript. These are not fatal, but they make reproduction and interpretation harder.
